parole.significato: A large African antelope (Addax nasomaculatus) with long, corkscrewing horns which lives in the desert.
parole.testo: From French addax, from Arabic أبو عدس (ʔabū ʕadas, literally “father of the lentil”).

parole.significato: A canoe made from tree bark, formerly used in Africa.
parole.testo: From French almadie (compare Spanish & Portuguese almadia), from Arabic مَعْدِيَة (maʕdiya, “ferry”).

parole.significato: A Turkish or Moroccan slipper having no heel.
parole.testo: From French babouche, from Arabic بَابُوش (bābūš), from Persian پاپوش (pâpuš, “slipper”).

parole.significato: A type of North African leather slippers used as general footwear.
parole.testo: From French balgha, from Arabic بَلْغَة (balḡa).

parole.significato: Synonym of nicker tree.
parole.testo: From French bonduc, from Arabic بُنْدُق (bunduq, “hazelnut, pebble, bullet”), from Middle Persian 𐭯𐭭𐭣𐭪 (pondik, “hazelnut”), from Ancient Greek Ποντικὸν κάρυον (Pontikòn káruon, “Pontic nut”). Doublet of bundook.

parole.significato: A thick hooded cloak worn by Berbers and Arabs in Northwest Africa.
parole.testo: From French burnous, from Arabic بُرْنُس (burnus).

parole.significato: A fern of species Asplenium ceterach.
parole.testo: From French cétérach, Arabic شطرك

parole.significato: A dry salt lake, in the Saharan area of Africa, that stays dry in the summer but receives some water in the winter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chott, from Arabic شَطّ (šaṭṭ). Some of the alternative forms/synonyms (shatt, shat) derive directly from Arabic.

parole.significato: A member of the Coptic Church.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French copte, from Arabic قُبْط (qubṭ, “Copts”), from Coptic ⲅⲩⲡⲧⲓⲟⲥ (guptios, “Egyptian”), ⲕⲩⲡⲧⲁⲓⲟⲥ (kuptaios, “Egyptian”), from Late Ancient Greek Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios), from earlier Αἴγυπτος (Aíguptos), from Egyptian Hwt-t:O1-kA:Z1-p:t-H-A40 (ḥwt-kꜣ-ptḥ, “Egypt; temple of Ptah's ka”

parole.significato: A pasta of North African origin made of crushed and steamed semolina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French couscous, from Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus), from a Berber language. First use appears c. 1593.

parole.significato: A protected and specially taxed non-Muslim subject of a state governed under dhimma, a form of social contract, in acco…
parole.testo: From French dhimmi, from Arabic ذِمِّيّ (ḏimmiyy, “a dhimmi”), from ذِمَّة (ḏimma, “protection, custody”).

parole.significato: A camp or village of tents in a North African country.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French douar, from Arabic دَوّار (dawwār).

parole.significato: A small fox of the species Vulpes zerda, found in the Sahara (excluding the coast) and having distinctive oversized ear…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fennec, from Arabic فَنَك (fanak).

parole.significato: To apply a dressing of gauze; to cover with gauze.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gaze, from Arabic قَزّ (qazz, “silk”).

parole.significato: A jinn, a being descended from the jann, normally invisible to the human eye, but who may also appear in animal or huma…
parole.testo: From French génie (“genius, genie”), a phono-semantic matching of Arabic جِنِّيّ (jinniyy).

parole.significato: A kind of saponifying vulcanic clay used for hair and skin care.
parole.testo: From French ghassoul, from Arabic غَاسُول (ḡāsūl).

parole.significato: A tent, hut or simple dwelling-place in North Africa, especially Algeria.
parole.testo: From French gourbi, from Arabic.

parole.significato: Chlamydotis undulata, a bustard, chiefly of North Africa and south-east Asia.
parole.testo: In this spelling, from French houbara, and later also directly from Arabic حُبَارَى (ḥubārā).

parole.significato: Any of several plants, of the genus Jasminum, mostly native to Asia, having fragrant white or yellow flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jasmin, from Arabic يَاسَمِين (yāsamīn).

parole.significato: A hill, a mountain (especially in the Middle East or North Africa).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French djebel, from Arabic جَبَل (jabal, “mountain”).

parole.significato: a fortified traditional village in North Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ksar, from a Maghrebi form of Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr). Doublet of qasr and castrum

parole.significato: A large shrub of the genus Syringa, especially Syringa vulgaris, bearing white, pale-pink, or purple flowers.
parole.testo: From obsolete French lilac (now lilas), from Arabic لِيلَك (līlak).

parole.significato: A sweet, light-coloured wine from Portugal.
parole.testo: As the capital of Portugal, from French Lisbonne, from Arabic لِشْبُونَة (lišbūna), from Latin Olisīpō, the origin of which is uncertain. Older spellings include Ulixbona and Ulixbuna (in the Visigothic era); Ὀλισσιπών (Olissipṓn) or Ὀλισσιπόνα (Olissipóna) (by Greek writers), Olisippo (by Pliny the

parole.significato: A balcony in North Africa enclosed with carved wooden latticework.
parole.testo: From French moucharaby, later reborrowed from its source, Arabic مَشْرَبِيَّة (mašrabiyya), from مِشْرَبَة (mišraba, “small jug”), from the water jars placed in it to provide evaporative cooling.

parole.significato: An underground storage place for grain.
parole.testo: From French matamore, from Arabic مَطْمُورَة (maṭmūra). Doublet of massymore.

parole.significato: A Maghrebi dish consisting of meat from a whole sheep or lamb spit-roasted on a barbecue.
parole.testo: From French méchoui, from Arabic مَشْوِيّ (mašwiyy).

parole.significato: open up (especially referring to doors)
parole.testo: From its use in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, translating French Sésame, ouvre-toi in Antoine Galland's version of the Ali Baba story in the One Thousand and One Nights, possibly based on an oral Arabic source. Not, as some have purported, a corruption of Open, says me!.

parole.significato: The currency of Mauritania, divided into five khoums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ouguiya, from Arabic أُوقِيَّة (ʔūqiyya), via Classical Syriac and Ancient Greek from Latin ū̆ncia (“ounce”). Doublet of ounce, inch, uncia, oka, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: A Middle Eastern dish made from acorns.
parole.testo: From French racahout, from Arabic راقوت.

parole.significato: A leguminous shrub (Sesbania aculeata or others of the genus Sesbania), whose fiber can be used for making ropes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sesban, from Arabic سَيْسَبَان (saysabān).

parole.significato: An ancient breed of domesticated dog, specifically a member of the sighthound family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sloughi, from dialectal Arabic سْلُوڭِي (slūgī, “greyhound”), from Arabic سَلُوقِيّ (salūqiyy, “greyhound”). Doublet of Saluki.

parole.significato: A raised area of a building's floor, usually covered with carpeting, used for sitting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sofa, ultimately from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa, “a long seat made of stone or brick, covered with rich carpets and cushions and used for sitting”). Cognate with Aramaic צפא/Classical Syriac ܨܦܬܐ (ṣipā’, ṣeppəṯā, “mat, matting”). The word may have entered European languages via Musli

parole.significato: A kind of waved silk, usually called watered silk, manufactured like taffeta, but thicker and stronger. The watering is…
parole.testo: Mid 17th century French tabis, from Arabic عَتَّابِيّ (ʕattābiyy), ultimately from Arabic الْعَتَّابِيَّة (al-ʕattābiyya), a quarter of Baghdad (named for a Prince عَتَّاب (ʕattāb)) which is associated with the manufacture of a certain type of waved silk. See also taffeta, another type of silk whose

parole.significato: A small gall formed on the tamarisk, used as a source of gallic acid.
parole.testo: From French tacahout m (“tacahout”), from Arabic تَاكُوت (tākūt), an early medieval Berber borrowing.

parole.significato: A magical object providing protection against ill will, or the supernatural, or conferring the wearer with a boon such…
parole.testo: From French talisman, partly from Arabic طِلَّسْم (ṭillasm, “payment”), from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “payment”); and partly directly from Byzantine Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “talisman, religious rite, completion”), from τελέω (teléō, “to perform religious rites, to complete”), from τέλος (télo

parole.significato: A small shallow drum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tambour (“drum”), from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr), from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور (tanbūr). Doublet of tabor and tanbur. Compare Armenian տաւիղ (tawiġ), and tabla.

parole.significato: A percussion instrument consisting of a small, usually wooden, hoop closed on one side with a drum frame and featuring…
parole.testo: From French tambourin (“little drum”), from French tambour (“drum”). Ultimately from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr); see it and Persian تنبور for more.

parole.significato: A cup or goblet for drinking wine.
parole.testo: From French tasse (“cup”), from Arabic طَاس (ṭās, “bowl, basin”).

parole.significato: The edible pine nuts of the Aleppo pine, used to make a variety of dishes.
parole.testo: From French zgougou, from Arabic زقوقو.

parole.significato: A good-for-nothing person.
parole.testo: Claimed by Swedish scholar Jan Ivarsson (quoted in Green's Dictionary of Slang) to derive from French zob (“dick, cock”), itself from Arabic زُبّ (zubb).

parole.significato: One of a body of soldiers in the French service, originally Kabyle, but now composed of Frenchmen who wear the Kabyle d…
parole.testo: From French, from Arabic زَوَاوِيّ (zawāwiyy), used to refer to a Kabyle soldier, especially of the Igawawen people.
